cl_gen_gateway.q: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs (the 'gateway' idea)?
cl_gen_gateway.short: Not known. These studies cannot show that cannabis itself caused later drug use.
cl_gen_gateway.but: Shared risks and access to drugs could still explain the link.
how: In New York schools in 1971 to 1972, about 1 in 4 students at the cannabis step tried another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4 in 100 who had used only legal drugs. The groups could differ in other ways.
In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used other drugs later. The comparison accounts for growing up in the same home, but not all genetic or other differences.
A computer model showed the same pattern appears if some people are simply more likely to use any drug and are offered cannabis first.
The order varied across countries. People sometimes used other illegal drugs without having used cannabis first, even in places where cannabis use was moderate.

cl_gen_polydrug.q: How common is using several drugs, and why does it matter?
cl_gen_polydrug.short: Common among people who use illegal drugs. It makes one drug's effects hard to study.
cl_gen_polydrug.but: Figures are second-hand, from two reviews, and vary hugely between groups.
how: A review cites Australian surveys in which 2 in 100 teenagers and about 13 in 100 young adults used a wide range of drugs. These were different groups, not the same people followed over time.
At underground raves, up to 75 in 100 people used several drugs, five on average at the last rave.
In ecstasy studies, 90 to 100 in 100 people also used cannabis, and many also drank alcohol or used stimulants.
A study of one drug may be measuring several drugs. Some older ecstasy studies did not record the other drugs.
